Neonates of the winter white dwarf hamster are altricial at birth, entering the world as hairless, blind pups with closed ear canals. The wet weight at birth is a mere 2 grams [Wwb = a mere 2 grams], a value that reflects the species' abbreviated intrauterine development. Juveniles undergo a period of rapid somatic growth sustained entirely by maternal milk during the suckling stage. The transition to nutritional independence, marking the nutritional emancipation of the offspring, occurs at 21 days since birth at weaning [tx = 21 days since birth at weaning] under the standard colony ambient temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. By this age, the pups have opened their eyes, developed a full coat, and begun consuming solid food. This relatively short suckling interval is typical for dwarf hamsters and facilitates the high reproductive turnover observed in the species.

Reproductive output in Phodopus sungorus is characterized by consistently sized litters and rapid sequential breeding events. Females produce an average of 5.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = an average of 5.5 pups per litter], a value that remains relatively invariant across successive parities. At the same body temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], they can achieve a maximum reproductive frequency of 3.5 litters per year [F_R_i = 3.5 litters per year], a substantial rate of population turnover for a rodent of this size class. The gestation time, spanning 20 days [tg = 20 days] at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], is notably condensed relative to other cricetid rodents, many of which require approximately four weeks to complete pregnancy. A post-partum estrus is the norm in this species, meaning that a female can be simultaneously lactating one litter while gestating the next, thereby compressing the inter-birth interval considerably.

Ultimate wet weight for males reaches approximately 30 grams [Wwi = approximately 30 grams], whereas females tend toward a slightly smaller final size. The overall adult body mass for the species, without sexual distinction, is reported in some compilations as 23.4 grams [Wwi = 23.4 grams], though field and captive data reveal substantial variation. Neonates, initially weighing 2 grams at parturition, increase their body mass by over seven-fold during the lactation period, so that by the time of weaning the wet weight at weaning is 14.8 grams [Wwx = 14.8 grams]. This rapid mass gain is fueled by the high caloric content of the mother's milk and positions the juvenile for a fast transition to the sub-adult growth phase.

The basal metabolic rate of Phodopus sungorus has been measured under strictly thermoneutral conditions. Resting oxygen consumption, recorded in a corrected table from the data of White and Seymour, is 40.9 milliliters per hour [JOi = 40.9 milliliters per hour] at a body temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This value represents the maximum basal metabolic rate documented for the species, aligning with the elevated metabolic demands typical of small-bodied endotherms inhabiting cold, semi-arid environments. The species relies on this relatively high metabolic output to sustain its rapid life-history schedule, including the energetic costs of gestation and the continuous milk production required for a fast-growing litter. Comparative data suggest that this mass-corrected metabolic rate is somewhat higher than the average for cricetid rodents of equivalent mass.

Under the standard captive conditions maintained at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], puberty is attained at 120 days since birth [tp = 120 days since birth], a timing that allows the animal to commence its first breeding season within the same calendar year of its own birth. The maximum documented lifespan is approximately 3.9 years [am = approximately 3.9 years], which is a comparatively moderate longevity for a rodent of its size and metabolic pace at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This combination of early maturation and a moderately extended lifespan enables the species to achieve a high lifetime reproductive output, with a single female capable of producing dozens of offspring across multiple litters under favorable conditions.
